differences.title: 1. Scheduling & batching
differences.leftDesc: vLLM uses PagedAttention to separate KV cache into pages, enabling continuous decoding across concurrent requests with minimal fragmentation. A scheduler batches tokens dynamically while preserving per-request attention correctness.
differences.rightDesc: TensorRT-LLM relies on NVIDIA TensorRT optimized graphs and plugins, typically favoring static, shape-informed execution paths. Throughput comes from kernel efficiency and batched GEMMs, with less emphasis on fine-grained token interleaving.

differences.title: 2. KV cache strategy
differences.leftDesc: vLLM allocates KV cache in fixed-size blocks and remaps them per sequence. This “paging” reduces wasted memory and supports many simultaneous sequence lengths by reusing blocks safely.
differences.rightDesc: TensorRT-LLM implements KV cache mechanics via TensorRT plugins and engine-specific memory layouts. The cache is managed to match the compiled kernels’ expectations, optimizing bandwidth and compute with constrained runtime flexibility.

differences.title: 3. Deployment model
differences.leftDesc: vLLM is commonly deployed as a Python-backed server that loads model weights and serves requests with runtime scheduling. You tune concurrency and memory limits without a full offline compilation step for every configuration.
differences.rightDesc: TensorRT-LLM uses an offline build step that compiles weights into TensorRT engines (often per precision and shape regime). Serving is then a lightweight runtime executing those prebuilt kernels for maximal performance predictability.

differences.title: 4. Precision & quantization
differences.leftDesc: vLLM supports multiple precisions and quantization workflows depending on model and backend settings, often selecting behavior at load/runtime. This makes experimentation and A/B performance tuning faster across deployments.
differences.rightDesc: TensorRT-LLM’s performance hinges on choosing precision (FP16/FP8/INT8 depending on platform) during engine build. Quantization parameters affect the compiled graph, so changes usually require rebuilding engines to regain peak throughput.

differences.title: 5. Operator coverage & model support
differences.leftDesc: vLLM targets high-level transformer inference behavior and typically supports a wide range of Hugging Face-style architectures via its attention and sampling stacks. Performance comes from memory efficiency rather than strict graph compilation.
differences.rightDesc: TensorRT-LLM depends on how well model layers map into TensorRT-supported ops and plugins. Unsupported patterns may fall back or require specific plugin implementations, making compatibility more engineering-sensitive.

differences.title: 6. Latency behavior under load
differences.leftDesc: Because vLLM can interleave token generation across requests using paged KV, it reduces “queueing latency” when many sequences are active. Tail latency often improves compared to batching-only approaches.
differences.rightDesc: TensorRT-LLM optimizes for high throughput with compiled kernels, so latency under mixed workloads can be dominated by batching/shape policies. When workload matches the engine’s ideal regime, latency is consistent and efficient.

differences.title: 7. Observability & tuning knobs
differences.leftDesc: vLLM exposes practical serving knobs like max sequence length, GPU memory utilization, and scheduling/concurrency behavior. Engineers can tune without recompiling, using metrics around token throughput and cache usage.
differences.rightDesc: TensorRT-LLM tuning spans both build-time and runtime: you adjust engine precision, optimization profiles, and plugin settings during compilation, then set batch/sequence execution parameters at serving for best kernel utilization.
